recipes.title: Apple Crumble
recipes.description: Sharp Bramley apples collapsing into their own juices under a craggy, buttery topping of flour, oats and demerara. Proper cold-weather pudding, best with custard.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 190°C (170°C fan). Have ready a baking dish of about 1.5 litres, roughly 20 x 28cm.

Peel, quarter and core the apples, then cut them into chunks about 2cm across. Toss them in the baking dish with the brown sugar, lemon juice, cinnamon and 2 tablespoons of water, then spread them out in an even layer.
steps.tip: Keep the pieces chunky. Bramleys break down a great deal, and thin slices will cook to a purée before the topping is done.

steps.text: Put the flour, salt and butter in a large bowl. Rub the butter in with your fingertips until the mixture looks like coarse, uneven breadcrumbs with some larger buttery lumps. Stir in the demerara sugar and the oats.
steps.tip: Squeeze a few handfuls of the mixture together and then break them up again. Those bigger nuggets are what bake into crunchy clusters.

steps.text: Scatter the topping loosely over the apples, right to the edges, without pressing it down.
Bake for 35–45 minutes, until the topping is deep golden and the fruit is bubbling up around the sides.
Leave the crumble to stand for 10 minutes before serving, so the juices thicken and nobody burns their mouth. Serve with custard, cream or vanilla ice cream.

tips: The topping can be made ahead and kept in a bag in the freezer. Scatter it over the fruit straight from frozen.
Taste a piece of apple before adding the sugar. Very sharp early-season Bramleys may want an extra tablespoon.

substitutions.note: reduce the sugar in the filling to 40g, as they are much sweeter and hold their shape
the crumble will no longer be nut-free

substitutions.use: a handful of blackberries added to the apples

recipes.storage: Cover and keep in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat at 180°C for 15–20 minutes to crisp the top again. The baked crumble freezes for up to 3 months.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Banana Bread
recipes.description: A soft, damp-crumbed loaf that tastes properly of banana, with brown sugar, a little cinnamon and a spoonful of yoghurt to keep it tender for days. The blacker the bananas, the better the loaf.

items.note: large and well speckled, about 300g peeled

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C (160°C fan). Butter a 900g (2lb) loaf tin and line it with a strip of baking paper that overhangs the two long sides, so you can lift the loaf out later.

Mash the bananas in a large bowl with a fork until mostly smooth, leaving a few small lumps. Whisk in the melted butter and sugar, then the eggs, yoghurt and vanilla, until you have a loose, even batter.
steps.tip: Bananas that are not ripe enough can be baked in their skins at 180°C for 15 minutes until black, then cooled and peeled.

steps.text: Sift the flour, bicarbonate of soda, baking powder, cinnamon and salt over the wet mixture. Fold together with a spatula, stopping as soon as the last streak of flour disappears. Fold in the walnuts, if using.
steps.tip: Overmixing is what makes banana bread tough and tunnelled — a slightly lumpy batter is exactly right.

steps.text: Scrape the batter into the tin and level the top. Bake on the middle shelf until well risen, deep golden and a skewer pushed into the centre comes out clean or with just a few moist crumbs, 55–65 minutes.
steps.tip: If the top is browning too quickly after 40 minutes, lay a sheet of foil loosely over it.

steps.text: Leave the loaf in its tin for 10 minutes, then lift it out by the paper onto a wire rack. Let it cool for at least 20 minutes more before slicing, as it firms up as it cools.

tips: The loaf is even better the day after baking, once the crumb has settled and the flavour has deepened.
A split banana laid cut-side up on the batter before baking makes a handsome top, though it will add about 5 minutes to the bake.

substitutions.note: the same weight
the loaf will be paler and a little less toffee-like

recipes.storage: Wrap well and keep at room temperature for up to 4 days. Freezes well for 3 months, whole or sliced; toast slices straight from frozen.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Basil Pesto
recipes.description: Vivid green and intensely fragrant, with toasted pine nuts, parmesan and just a whisper of garlic. Made in short pulses so the basil stays bright and the texture stays coarse.

steps.text: Toast the pine nuts in a small dry frying pan over a medium-low heat, shaking often, until pale gold. Tip onto a plate straight away and leave to cool completely.
steps.tip: Do not walk away. Pine nuts go from golden to burnt in seconds, and they carry on colouring if left in the hot pan.

steps.text: Put the cooled pine nuts, garlic and salt in a food processor and pulse to a coarse crumb.
Add the basil and pulse in short bursts, scraping down the sides once or twice, until finely chopped but not puréed.
steps.tip: Short pulses matter. Running the motor continuously heats the leaves, which turns the pesto dark and slightly bitter.

steps.text: Add the parmesan and pulse briefly to combine. Scrape into a bowl and stir in the olive oil by hand until you have a loose, spoonable sauce. Taste and add more salt if needed.

To use with pasta, take the drained pasta off the heat and toss it with the pesto and a few tablespoons of the starchy cooking water until it coats glossily. This quantity dresses about 400 g of dried pasta.

tips: Never cook pesto. Direct heat dulls the basil and makes the cheese clump, so always combine it with pasta off the heat.
With a pestle and mortar, pound the garlic and salt first, then the pine nuts, then the basil a handful at a time, and finally work in the cheese and oil. It takes longer but gives a creamier result.

substitutions.note: toast them in the same way
or half and half; pecorino is saltier, so hold back on the salt

recipes.storage: Spoon into a small jar, level the top and cover with a thin layer of olive oil. Keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days, or freeze in an ice-cube tray for up to 3 months.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Slow-Cooked Beef Ragù with Tagliatelle
recipes.description: Chunks of beef braised in red wine and tomato until they fall apart under a spoon, then tossed through ribbons of tagliatelle. Mostly hands-off, and better still the next day.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C (140°C fan). Pat the beef dry with kitchen paper and season it well with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a large casserole over a medium-high heat and brown the beef in two or three batches, turning until it is deep brown on most sides. Lift each batch out onto a plate.
steps.tip: Do not crowd the pan. Beef that touches steams instead of browning, and the browning is where the flavour comes from.

steps.text: Turn the heat down to medium. Add the onion, carrots and celery with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring now and then and scraping up the sticky bits from the base, until soft and lightly golden.
Stir in the garlic and tomato puree and cook until the puree darkens a shade and smells sweet rather than raw.

Pour in the wine, turn up the heat and let it bubble until reduced by about half. Add the chopped tomatoes, stock, bay leaves and rosemary, then return the beef and any juices from the plate. Bring to a gentle simmer.
Cover with a tight-fitting lid and cook in the oven until the beef collapses when pressed with a spoon. Check once, around the two-hour mark, and add a splash of water if it looks dry.

Fish out the bay leaves and rosemary stalks. Shred the beef into the sauce with two forks. If the ragù is loose, simmer it on the hob without the lid until it is thick enough to coat a spoon. Taste and season.
Cook the tagliatelle in a large pot of well-salted boiling water until just al dente, following the packet timing. Scoop out a mugful of the cooking water, then drain.

Tip the pasta into the ragù with the butter, parmesan and a good splash of pasta water. Toss over a low heat for a minute until the sauce is glossy and clings to the ribbons. Serve with more parmesan.
steps.tip: If your casserole will not hold all the pasta, toss it in the empty pasta pot with as much ragù as you need.

tips: Shin gives the silkiest sauce because of its connective tissue. Chuck is leaner and a little quicker to soften.
The ragù improves overnight in the fridge. Reheat it gently with a splash of water before cooking the pasta.

substitutions.note: add 1 tbsp balsamic vinegar for acidity

recipes.storage: The ragù keeps for 4 days in the fridge or 3 months in the freezer, without the pasta. Defrost fully and reheat until piping hot.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Brown Butter Miso Pasta
recipes.description: Nutty brown butter and white miso emulsified with pasta water into a glossy, deeply savoury sauce. Fifteen minutes, a handful of ingredients.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of water to the boil and salt it lightly — the miso brings plenty of salt of its own. Cook the spaghetti until a minute shy of al dente.
steps.tip: Scoop out a mugful of the starchy cooking water before you drain.

steps.text: While the pasta cooks, melt the butter in a wide frying pan over a medium heat. Keep it moving until it foams, smells of toasted hazelnuts and the milk solids turn amber.
Take the pan off the heat. Stir in the garlic, then whisk in the miso with a splash of pasta water until smooth.
Add the drained spaghetti and parmesan to the pan and return to a low heat. Toss hard, adding pasta water a little at a time, until the sauce is glossy and clings to every strand.
Pile into warm bowls and finish with spring onions, more parmesan and a heavy grind of black pepper.

tips: Use a pale pan if you have one so you can see the butter change colour.

substitutions.note: use a little less, it is saltier

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away; the sauce tightens as it cools.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Buttermilk Pancakes
recipes.description: Thick, tender pancakes with crisp golden edges and a gentle tang from the buttermilk. A lumpy batter and a short rest are the whole secret.

steps.text: Whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder, bicarbonate of soda and salt together in a large bowl so the raising agents are evenly spread.

In a jug, beat the buttermilk and eggs together, then whisk in the melted butter. Pour the wet mixture into the dry and fold with a spatula just until no dry flour remains. The batter should be thick and lumpy.
steps.tip: Stop mixing while it still looks rough. Beating out the lumps develops the gluten and makes the pancakes tough and flat.

steps.text: Leave the batter to stand while you heat the pan. It will puff up and thicken; do not stir it again.
Set a large non-stick frying pan or griddle over a medium-low heat for a couple of minutes. Wipe it with a little oil on a piece of kitchen paper so there is only a thin film.
steps.tip: The first pancake tells you about the heat. If it is dark before bubbles appear on top, turn the hob down.

steps.text: Drop in heaped serving spoons of batter, about 4 tbsp each, leaving room to spread. Cook until the edges look matt and bubbles are breaking across the surface, then flip and cook until the second side is golden and the middle springs back when pressed.

Keep the cooked pancakes warm in a single layer in a low oven (100°C, 80°C fan) while you cook the rest, wiping the pan with more oil between batches. Serve in stacks with maple syrup and a little butter.

tips: If your buttermilk is very thick and the batter will not drop off the spoon, loosen it with 2–3 tbsp of milk.
Scatter blueberries or sliced banana onto each pancake in the pan rather than stirring them through the batter, so they stay evenly spread and do not stain it.

substitutions.use: 300 g natural yoghurt thinned with 100 ml milk
400 ml whole milk mixed with 1½ tbsp lemon juice
substitutions.note: leave for 10 minutes to thicken; the batter will be a little thinner

recipes.storage: Cool completely, then keep in the fridge for up to 2 days or freeze between sheets of baking paper for up to 2 months. Reheat in the toaster or a dry pan.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Buttermilk Scones
recipes.description: Tall, tender scones with a soft crumb and a faint tang from the buttermilk, on the table in half an hour. A light hand and a hot oven are all they ask for.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 220°C (200°C fan) and put a large baking tray inside to heat up.
steps.tip: A hot tray gives the scones an immediate burst of heat from below, which helps them rise straight up.

steps.text: Sift the flour, baking powder and salt into a large bowl. Add the butter and rub it in with your fingertips until the mixture looks like fine breadcrumbs with a few pea-sized pieces left. Stir in the sugar.

Make a well in the middle and pour in the buttermilk. Mix quickly with a table knife, cutting through the mixture, until it just comes together into a soft, slightly sticky dough. If dry flour remains in the bottom of the bowl, add another tablespoon of buttermilk.
steps.tip: Stop mixing the moment it holds together. Every extra stir develops gluten and makes for a tougher scone.

steps.text: Tip the dough onto a lightly floured worktop and fold it over on itself two or three times until it is just smooth. Pat it out with your hands to a round about 3cm thick; do not use a rolling pin.
Dip a 6cm round cutter in flour and stamp out the scones, pressing straight down without twisting. Gently press the trimmings together and cut again; you should get 8 in total.
steps.tip: Twisting the cutter seals the edges and the scones will rise lopsided.

steps.text: Brush just the tops with beaten egg, keeping it off the sides. Arrange on the hot tray and bake for 12–15 minutes, until well risen and golden.
Cool on a wire rack for a few minutes. Serve warm or at room temperature, split by hand, with jam and clotted cream.

tips: Keep the butter and buttermilk cold and work fast, so the butter stays in small pieces until it reaches the oven.
Scones are at their best within a few hours of baking. Day-old ones revive well after 5 minutes in a 160°C oven.

substitutions.use: 170ml whole milk mixed with 2 tsp lemon juice
substitutions.note: leave to stand for 5 minutes until slightly thickened

substitutions.use: 75g sultanas as well as the sugar
substitutions.note: stirred in before the buttermilk for fruit scones

recipes.storage: Best eaten on the day. Freeze once cooled for up to 3 months, then defrost and warm through in the oven.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Caesar Salad
recipes.description: Cold, crisp romaine and craggy oven-baked croutons in a punchy dressing of anchovy, garlic, lemon and parmesan, whisked by hand in the bottom of the salad bowl.

items.note: a day or two old is ideal

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200°C (180°C fan). Toss the torn bread with the olive oil and salt on a baking tray, squeezing the pieces lightly so they soak up the oil.
Bake, shaking the tray halfway through, until deep golden and crisp outside with a little chew left in the middle. Leave to cool on the tray.
Chop the anchovies and garlic together on a board, then crush them to a paste with the flat of the knife. Scrape into a large salad bowl.
steps.tip: A pinch of salt on the board gives the knife some grit and makes the paste come together faster.

steps.text: Whisk in the egg yolk, mustard, lemon juice and Worcestershire sauce. Whisking all the time, add the vegetable oil a few drops at a time at first, then in a thin stream as the dressing thickens, followed by the extra virgin olive oil.
steps.tip: Sit the bowl on a damp cloth to stop it spinning. If the dressing gets too thick to whisk, loosen it with a teaspoon of water.

steps.text: Whisk in the grated parmesan and a lot of black pepper. Taste on a piece of lettuce — it should be sharp, salty and savoury — and add more lemon if needed.
Tear any large lettuce leaves in half, leaving the small inner ones whole. Add to the bowl and turn them over gently with your hands until every leaf is coated.
Add the croutons, toss once more, and finish with the parmesan shavings and another grind of pepper. Serve immediately.

tips: The dressing contains raw egg yolk. Use the freshest eggs you can (British Lion-stamped in the UK), or see the substitution below if you are cooking for anyone pregnant, elderly or unwell.
Dry the lettuce thoroughly. Water on the leaves stops the dressing clinging and thins it out.

substitutions.note: whisk the other dressing ingredients into it, including the olive oil

substitutions.use: ciabatta or any crusty white loaf

recipes.storage: Dress only what you will eat. The dressing keeps covered in the fridge for 2 days and the croutons in an airtight tin for 3 days.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Chicken Noodle Soup
recipes.description: Chicken thighs poached on the bone in a broth of carrot, celery and thyme, shredded back in with fine egg noodles, parsley and a squeeze of lemon. Restorative in the plainest sense.

items.prep: peeled and sliced into thin rounds

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large saucepan over a medium heat. Add the onion, carrots and celery with a pinch of salt and cook gently, stirring now and then, until softened but not coloured.
Stir in the garlic and cook for 1 minute. Nestle in the chicken thighs, then add the stock, thyme and bay leaf.
Bring just to the boil, skim off any foam, then turn the heat right down, cover with the lid ajar and simmer very gently until the chicken is cooked through and pulls easily from the bone.
steps.tip: Keep it at a lazy simmer. A hard boil turns the broth cloudy and the meat stringy.

steps.text: Lift the chicken onto a board. Fish out and discard the thyme stalks and bay leaf. Shred the meat with two forks and throw away the bones.
Bring the broth back to a simmer, add the noodles and cook until just tender, usually 3–4 minutes — check the packet.
Return the chicken to the pan and warm through for a minute. Stir in the parsley and lemon juice, then season with salt and plenty of black pepper before ladling into warm bowls.

tips: If you are making this ahead, cook the noodles separately and add them to each bowl. Left sitting in the soup they drink the broth and go soft.

substitutions.note: add with the noodles and simmer the broth for only 15 minutes

substitutions.use: broken spaghetti or small soup pasta
substitutions.note: allow a few minutes longer

recipes.storage: Keeps for 3 days in the fridge, ideally with noodles stored separately. Freeze without noodles for up to 3 months and reheat until piping hot.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Chickpea and Spinach Curry
recipes.description: A gently spiced, coconut-rich curry built from tins and a bag of spinach. Crushing a few of the chickpeas into the sauce makes it thick and velvety without any cream.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, deep pan over a medium heat. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring often, until soft and golden at the edges.
steps.tip: Do not rush this. Properly golden onions give the sauce its sweetness and body.

steps.text: Stir in the garlic, ginger and green chilli and cook until fragrant. Add the cumin, ground coriander, turmeric and chilli powder and stir for 30 seconds more, adding a splash of water if the spices start to catch.
Tip in the chopped tomatoes and cook, stirring, until they have thickened into a paste and the oil starts to show around the edges.
Add the chickpeas, coconut milk and salt. Bring to a simmer and cook uncovered, stirring now and then, until the sauce has thickened. Meanwhile, cook the rice following the packet instructions.
Crush roughly a quarter of the chickpeas against the side of the pan with the back of a spoon and stir them in to thicken the sauce.
Add the spinach a handful at a time, stirring until each addition wilts, then stir in the garam masala and cook briefly.
Take off the heat, stir in the lemon juice, then taste and adjust the salt. Serve over the rice, scattered with coriander.

tips: Garam masala goes in at the end so its aromatic spices stay bright rather than cooking out.
If the curry gets too thick, loosen it with a splash of water. It should be spoonable, not stiff.

substitutions.note: use 250g, add from frozen and simmer for 5 minutes
the dish is then no longer gluten-free

recipes.storage: Keeps for 4 days in the fridge and freezes well for 3 months, without the rice. Reheat until piping hot, adding a splash of water.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Chilli and Garlic Prawn Linguine
recipes.description: Sweet prawns, slow-sizzled garlic and fresh chilli tossed through linguine with burst cherry tomatoes, white wine and lemon. The sauce is ready before the pasta is.

items.note: plus a little extra to finish

items.prep: deseeded if you like, finely chopped

steps.text: Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil. Cook the linguine until a minute shy of al dente, as it will finish cooking in the sauce.
steps.tip: Scoop out a mugful of the starchy cooking water before you drain.

steps.text: While the pasta cooks, put the oil, garlic and chilli into a wide, cold frying pan and set it over a medium-low heat. Let them sizzle gently until the garlic is soft and fragrant but not coloured.
steps.tip: Starting in a cold pan flavours the oil and makes it much harder to burn the garlic, which would turn the whole dish bitter.

steps.text: Add the cherry tomatoes with a pinch of salt and cook until they start to slump and release their juices.
Turn the heat up to medium-high. Add the prawns in a single layer and cook for about a minute on each side, until they have just turned pink all over.
Pour in the wine and let it bubble for a minute to cook off the alcohol.
Add the drained linguine and a good splash of the pasta water. Toss vigorously over the heat for a minute until the sauce turns glossy and coats the pasta, adding more water if it looks dry.
Take off the heat and toss through the lemon zest, lemon juice and parsley. Season with salt and pepper, divide between warm bowls and finish with a drizzle of olive oil.

tips: Prawns turn rubbery fast. They are done as soon as they are pink and curled into a loose C shape.
If using frozen prawns, defrost them fully in the fridge and dry them well, or they will stew in their own water.

substitutions.note: add an extra squeeze of lemon
about half a teaspoon

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away. Reheated prawns toughen, so this is not one for leftovers.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Chimichurri
recipes.description: A sharp, garlicky Argentinian sauce of hand-chopped parsley, oregano, chilli and red wine vinegar loosened with olive oil. Spoon it over grilled steak, chicken, fish or roast vegetables.

items.prep: leaves and fine stalks, finely chopped

steps.text: Put the garlic, oregano, chilli flakes and salt in a bowl. Pour over the vinegar and warm water, stir, and leave to stand so the dried herbs and chilli rehydrate and the vinegar takes the raw edge off the garlic.
Meanwhile wash the parsley and dry it thoroughly, then chop it finely with a sharp knife. Discard only the thick lower stalks.
steps.tip: Chop by hand rather than using a food processor. A blade bruises the leaves into a murky paste; a knife keeps the sauce loose, green and textured.

steps.text: Stir the parsley into the vinegar mixture, then stir in the olive oil. The sauce should be loose and spoonable, with the herbs suspended in the oil rather than blended into it.
Leave at room temperature for the flavours to come together, then taste and adjust with salt, pepper or a few more drops of vinegar. Stir well before serving, as it separates on standing.

tips: Wet parsley makes a watery sauce that spoils quickly, so dry it properly in a salad spinner or a clean tea towel before chopping.
Use half as a marinade for steak or chicken and keep the other half, untouched by raw meat, to serve at the table.

substitutions.note: deseeded and finely chopped

recipes.storage: Keeps in a sealed jar in the fridge for up to 5 days; the colour dulls after the first day but the flavour holds. Bring to room temperature and stir before using, as the oil sets when cold.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Chocolate Chip Cookies
recipes.description: Crisp at the edge, soft and chewy in the middle, with puddles of dark chocolate and a little flaky salt on top. Melted butter means no creaming and no mixer.

steps.text: Melt the butter in a small pan over a low heat, then pour it into a large bowl and leave it for 5 minutes so it is warm rather than hot.
Add both sugars to the butter and whisk for a full minute until thick and glossy. Whisk in the egg, egg yolk and vanilla until the mixture is smooth and looks like loose caramel.
Tip in the flour, bicarbonate of soda and fine salt and stir with a spatula until only a few floury streaks remain. Add the chocolate and fold until evenly distributed and no dry flour is left.
Cover the bowl and chill the dough for 30 minutes, until firm enough to scoop. Meanwhile, heat the oven to 180°C (160°C fan) and line two large baking trays with baking paper.
steps.tip: Chilling stops the cookies spreading into thin discs. A longer rest of up to 48 hours in the fridge gives a deeper, more toffee-like flavour.

steps.text: Roll the dough into 16 balls of about 50g each. Space eight on each tray, leaving at least 5cm between them, and sprinkle each with a little flaky salt if you like.
Bake for 11–13 minutes, until the edges are golden and set but the centres still look pale and slightly underdone. If your oven heats unevenly, swap the trays halfway through.
steps.tip: Take them out sooner than seems right. They carry on cooking on the hot tray, and that is where the chewy middle comes from.

steps.text: Leave the cookies on their trays for 10 minutes to firm up, then move them to a wire rack to cool completely.

tips: Chop a bar of chocolate rather than using chips — the mix of shards and chunks melts into layers through the dough.
Shaped dough balls freeze well. Bake them from frozen, adding 2 minutes to the time.

substitutions.use: milk chocolate or a mixture of the two

substitutions.note: for a stronger treacle flavour and a softer cookie

recipes.storage: Keep in an airtight tin for up to 5 days. Freeze unbaked dough balls for up to 3 months.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Crispy Roast Potatoes
recipes.description: Glassy, deep-gold crusts around fluffy middles. The method is simple but strict — parboil until the edges fray, rough them up, and get them into properly hot oil.

items.note: such as Maris Piper or King Edward

steps.text: Heat the oven to 220°C (200°C fan). Peel the potatoes and cut them into even pieces roughly the size of a small egg, aiming for plenty of flat sides and sharp corners.

Put the potatoes in a large pan, cover with cold water and add the tablespoon of salt. Bring to the boil, then simmer until the outsides are soft and starting to break up but a knife still meets resistance in the centre.
steps.tip: Start timing from when the water reaches a simmer. Undercooked edges will not rough up, and that rough surface is what turns crisp.

steps.text: Drain in a colander and leave to steam dry. Meanwhile pour the oil into a large, heavy roasting tin and put it in the oven to heat.
Shake the colander firmly several times until the potatoes are scuffed all over and coated in a thin, fluffy paste of their own starch.

Carefully take the hot tin out of the oven and set it on the hob or a heatproof surface. Add the potatoes one by one — they should sizzle on contact — and turn each to coat in oil. Space them out so none are touching, then roast, turning them once halfway through.
steps.tip: Crowded potatoes steam instead of roast. If they do not fit in one layer with gaps, use a second tin.

steps.text: Turn the potatoes again, tuck in the garlic and rosemary and roast until deep golden and crisp on every side.
Lift out with a slotted spoon, leaving the oil behind, and scatter with flaky sea salt. Serve at once.

tips: You can parboil, rough up and cool the potatoes up to a day ahead. Keep them uncovered in the fridge; the drier surface roasts even crisper. Allow an extra 5–10 minutes in the oven.
Waxy or new potatoes will not fluff up at the edges, so choose a floury variety.

substitutions.use: goose fat, duck fat or beef dripping
substitutions.note: richer flavour, but the dish is then no longer vegetarian

recipes.storage: Best straight from the oven. Leftovers keep in the fridge for 2 days; reheat on a tray at 220°C (200°C fan) for 10–15 minutes to crisp up again.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Crunchy Peanut Noodle Salad
recipes.description: Cold rice noodles and a heap of shredded raw vegetables tossed in a lime, ginger and peanut dressing, finished with herbs and roasted peanuts. Travels well, so it makes a fine packed lunch.

items.note: 1 juiced, 1 cut into wedges to serve

items.prep: peeled and cut into thin matchsticks
deseeded and cut into thin batons

steps.text: Whisk the peanut butter, soy sauce, lime juice, rice vinegar, maple syrup, 1 tbsp sesame oil, ginger, garlic and sriracha in a large bowl. Add the warm water a spoonful at a time until the dressing pours like double cream.
steps.tip: Peanut butters vary in thickness. Stop adding water as soon as the dressing runs off the whisk in a ribbon.

steps.text: Put the noodles and edamame in a heatproof bowl, cover generously with boiling water and leave until the noodles are tender — usually 3–4 minutes, but check the packet.

Drain into a colander and rinse under cold running water until completely cool. Shake very dry, then toss with the extra 1 tsp sesame oil and snip through the noodles a few times with scissors so they are easier to mix and eat.

Add the cabbage, carrots, pepper, cucumber and most of the spring onions to the bowl of dressing, followed by the noodles and edamame. Toss thoroughly with tongs or clean hands until everything is coated.
Fold through most of the coriander and mint. Pile onto a platter or into bowls and finish with the peanuts and the rest of the herbs and spring onions. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing.

tips: For a packed lunch, keep the peanuts separate and add them just before eating so they stay crunchy.
The noodles absorb dressing as they sit. If you make it ahead, hold back a few spoonfuls to loosen it before serving.

substitutions.note: makes the dish gluten-free if your noodles are pure rice
cook according to the packet; egg noodles are not vegan

recipes.storage: Keeps for 2 days in an airtight container in the fridge. Loosen with a squeeze of lime before eating.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Dark Chocolate Mousse
recipes.description: The classic French method with no cream — just dark chocolate lightened with whisked egg whites, for a mousse that is airy on the spoon and intensely chocolatey.

items.note: very fresh and at room temperature

steps.text: Put the chocolate and butter in a large heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water, without letting the bowl touch the water. Stir occasionally until smooth and glossy, then lift the bowl off the pan and leave to cool for 8–10 minutes, until just warm.
steps.tip: Keep every drop of water and steam out of the chocolate, or it can seize into a grainy paste.

steps.text: Beat the egg yolks into the warm chocolate one at a time with a spatula. The mixture will thicken and turn shiny. If it looks stiff or dull, beat in a tablespoon of warm water to loosen it.

In a spotlessly clean bowl, whisk the egg whites with the salt until they form soft peaks. Add the sugar a spoonful at a time, whisking between additions, until the whites are glossy and hold a peak that just flops at the tip.
steps.tip: Stop before the whites become dry and clumpy. Over-whisked whites will not fold in smoothly and leave white flecks in the mousse.

steps.text: Stir a third of the whites firmly into the chocolate to slacken it. Add the rest in two batches, folding gently with a large metal spoon or spatula — cut down through the middle, sweep along the bottom and turn the mixture over — until no white streaks remain.
Spoon into four small glasses or ramekins, cover and chill for at least 3 hours, until set.
Take the mousses out of the fridge 10 minutes before serving to take the chill off. Serve as they are or with a spoonful of softly whipped cream.

tips: This mousse contains raw eggs, so use the freshest you can (British Lion-stamped in the UK) and do not serve it to anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or unwell.
Chocolate above about 75% cocoa solids can make the mousse stiff and grainy. Around 70% is the sweet spot.

substitutions.note: makes the mousse dairy-free if your chocolate is too

recipes.storage: Keep covered in the fridge and eat within 2 days. Not suitable for freezing.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Fish Tacos with Lime Slaw
recipes.description: Smoky spice-rubbed white fish, flaked into warm corn tortillas with a sharp lime and coriander slaw, avocado and a cooling soured cream sauce.

steps.text: Juice the two slaw limes and set aside 1 tbsp of the juice for the crema. Put the cabbage in a large bowl with the lime zest, the rest of the juice, the salt and sugar. Scrunch hard with your hands for a minute until it starts to soften and turn bright pink, then leave to sit.
Stir the soured cream, mayonnaise, hot sauce and reserved lime juice together in a small bowl. Taste and add more hot sauce if you like.

Pat the fish very dry with kitchen paper and cut into strips about 3 cm wide. Mix the cumin, smoked paprika, chilli powder, garlic powder and salt, then turn the fish gently in the spices and 1 tbsp of the oil until evenly coated.

Heat the remaining oil in a large non-stick frying pan over a medium-high heat. Lay in the fish and cook without moving it until the underside is browned, about 3 minutes, then turn carefully and cook for 2 minutes more, until opaque all the way through and just starting to flake.
steps.tip: Cook in two batches if the pan is crowded, otherwise the fish steams and will not take on colour.

steps.text: Warm the tortillas one or two at a time in a dry frying pan over a high heat for about 30 seconds a side, until soft and lightly toasted in spots. Stack them in a clean tea towel to keep warm.
Stir the spring onions and coriander through the slaw. Fill each tortilla with slaw, a few pieces of fish and some avocado, spoon over the crema and serve with lime wedges.

tips: Corn tortillas crack if they are not properly warmed. Heat them just before serving and keep them wrapped.
Choose thick fillets where you can. Thin tail pieces cook in half the time and break up easily.

substitutions.note: cook for 1–2 minutes a side until pink

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. The slaw, without the herbs, and the crema both keep for 2 days in the fridge; cooked fish keeps for 1 day and is good cold.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: French Omelette
recipes.description: A pale, smooth omelette rolled around a soft, custardy middle, with no browning at all. Three eggs, a knob of butter and about two minutes of your full attention.

steps.text: Crack the eggs into a bowl, add the salt and beat with a fork until completely uniform, with no streaks of white left. Have a warm plate, the chives and a heatproof spatula next to the hob; once the eggs go in there is no time to fetch anything.
steps.tip: Beat thoroughly but do not whip. You want the eggs blended, not frothy.

steps.text: Put a 20 cm non-stick frying pan over a medium-low heat and add the butter. Swirl until it has melted and is foaming gently. If it starts to colour, lift the pan off the heat for a moment.

Pour in the eggs. Stir continuously in small circles with the spatula while shaking the pan back and forth with your other hand, scraping the sides as you go, until the eggs have formed very small, soft curds and look like loose, creamy scrambled egg with a thin layer still liquid on top. This takes 1–1½ minutes.
steps.tip: If the curds are forming in large lumps, the pan is too hot. Lift it off the heat and keep stirring.

steps.text: Stop stirring, smooth the eggs into an even layer and leave the pan still for about 10 seconds so the underside just sets into a thin skin. Take the pan off the heat.

Tilt the pan away from you and use the spatula to fold the third nearest the handle over the middle. Tap the pan so the omelette slides to the far edge, then roll it out onto the warm plate so it lands seam-side down.
Tuck in the ends to neaten the shape, rub the top with a little cold butter for shine, and finish with the chives and a pinch of white pepper. Eat immediately.

tips: The pan matters more than anything else. A scratched or oversized pan makes rolling very difficult; 20 cm is right for three eggs.
The centre is meant to be soft and barely set. If you prefer it firmer, leave it in the pan for another 20–30 seconds before rolling.

substitutions.note: it will show as dark flecks but tastes just as good

recipes.storage: Does not keep; make it and eat it straight away.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: French Onion Soup
recipes.description: A kilo of onions cooked low and slow until dark and jammy, simmered in beef stock and wine, then capped with garlicky toasts and a blistered lid of gruyère.

steps.text: Melt the butter with the oil in a large, heavy casserole over a medium-low heat. Add the onions and a good pinch of salt, stir to coat, then cover and let them sweat until soft and collapsed.
Take the lid off, stir in the sugar and turn the heat up to medium. Cook, stirring every few minutes and scraping the base of the pan, until the onions are a deep chestnut brown and sticky.
steps.tip: If the onions catch before they colour evenly, add a splash of water and scrape up the dark bits — that is flavour, not a mistake.

steps.text: Stir in the sliced garlic and thyme and cook for 2 minutes. Sprinkle over the flour and stir for another minute to cook it out.
Pour in the wine and let it bubble for 2–3 minutes, scraping the base of the pan clean. Add the stock and bay leaf, bring to the boil, then turn down and simmer with the lid ajar.
Meanwhile, heat the grill to high. Toast the baguette slices on both sides until crisp and golden, then rub one side of each with the cut garlic clove.
Fish out the bay leaf, stir in the brandy if using, and season the soup well with salt and pepper. Ladle into four ovenproof bowls set on a baking tray.

Float two toasts on each bowl, pile the gruyère over the top and slide under the grill until the cheese is molten and blistered in places. Leave to stand for a couple of minutes before serving — the bowls will be very hot.

tips: The colour of the onions is the colour of the soup. Do not rush them; the full 40 minutes is what makes this taste like the real thing.
No ovenproof bowls? Grill the cheese on the toasts on a tray and float them on the soup at the table.

substitutions.note: add 1 tsp soy sauce for depth

recipes.storage: The soup, without toasts, keeps for 3 days in the fridge or 3 months in the freezer. Reheat until piping hot and make the cheese toasts fresh.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Fudgy Brownies
recipes.description: Dense, dark and squidgy in the middle with a paper-thin crackled top. Whisking the eggs and sugar until pale is the small effort that gives them their shine.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C (160°C fan). Butter a 20cm square tin and line the base and sides with baking paper, leaving some overhang to lift the brownies out.

Put the chocolate and butter in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water, making sure the bowl does not touch the water. Stir now and then until melted and smooth, then take off the heat and leave to cool for 10 minutes.
steps.tip: The chocolate should feel only just warm when you use it. If it is hot it will scramble the eggs and deflate the foam.

steps.text: In a large bowl, whisk the eggs, sugar and vanilla with an electric whisk for 3–4 minutes, until pale, thick and almost doubled in volume. The mixture should fall from the beaters in a ribbon that sits on the surface for a second or two.

Pour the cooled chocolate around the edge of the egg mixture and fold it through gently with a large spatula. Sift over the flour, cocoa and salt and fold again, just until the batter is evenly dark with no pale streaks.

Scrape the batter into the tin and level it into the corners. Bake for 22–26 minutes, until the top is shiny and crackled and the middle has only the faintest wobble. A skewer should come out with damp, sticky crumbs, not wet batter and not clean.
steps.tip: Start checking at 22 minutes. An overbaked brownie turns cakey and there is no way back.

steps.text: Leave the brownies to cool completely in the tin, at least 90 minutes, then lift out and cut into 16 squares with a large sharp knife, wiping the blade between cuts.
steps.tip: For very neat squares, chill the cooled slab for an hour before cutting.

tips: Brownies are noticeably fudgier the day after baking, so they are a good thing to make ahead.
A whisk by hand will work for the eggs and sugar, but allow 6–8 minutes of vigorous whisking.

substitutions.note: makes them gluten-free and a little denser, but no longer nut-free

substitutions.use: half caster and half light brown sugar
substitutions.note: for a chewier brownie with a duller top

recipes.storage: Keep in an airtight tin for up to 5 days. Freeze, wrapped, for up to 3 months.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Garlic Green Beans
recipes.description: Bright, squeaky-tender green beans tossed in olive oil with slivers of golden garlic and a squeeze of lemon. On the table in ten minutes and good beside almost anything.

steps.text: Bring a large pan of well-salted water to a rolling boil. Add the beans and cook until bright green and just tender, with a slight bite left in the middle.
steps.tip: Fine beans need about 3 minutes, thicker ones up to 5. Bite one to check.

steps.text: Drain thoroughly and leave in the colander for a minute to steam dry, so they fry rather than spit when they meet the oil.
Put the oil and garlic in a wide frying pan and set over a medium-low heat. Cook gently, stirring, until the garlic is pale gold and fragrant, then add the chilli flakes if using.
steps.tip: Starting the garlic in cold oil gives you more control. Take it no further than light gold; brown garlic tastes bitter.

steps.text: Turn the heat up to medium-high, add the beans and toss for a minute or two until hot and glossy. Take off the heat, add the lemon juice, season with salt and pepper and serve straight away.

tips: To get ahead, boil the beans, cool them quickly under cold running water and dry well. Finish them in the garlic oil just before serving, allowing an extra minute to heat through.
Add the lemon juice only at the end; acid dulls the green colour if it sits.

substitutions.note: adjust the boiling time until just tender
no longer vegan or dairy-free

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Leftovers keep in the fridge for 2 days and are good cold in a salad.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Ginger Pork Noodles
recipes.description: Pork mince fried until crisp at the edges, tossed with egg noodles, greens and a punchy soy and ginger sauce. A fast stir-fry where the prep takes longer than the cooking.

items.prep: peeled and cut into fine matchsticks
sliced, whites and greens kept separate

steps.text: Stir the sauce ingredients together in a small bowl until the cornflour has dissolved. Prepare all the vegetables and have everything within reach of the hob, because nothing waits once the cooking starts.

Cook the noodles in boiling water following the packet timing, until just tender. Drain, rinse briefly under cold water to stop them cooking, then toss with the sesame oil so they do not stick together.

Heat a wok or large frying pan over a high heat until very hot, then add the vegetable oil. Add the pork, press it out into a thin layer and leave it without stirring until the underside is browned and crisp.
steps.tip: Resist the urge to stir straight away. Mince that is kept moving releases its liquid and stews.

steps.text: Break the pork into small pieces and keep frying until it is cooked through with crisp, golden edges.
Add the ginger, garlic, spring onion whites and the chilli if using. Stir-fry for 30 seconds, then add the carrot and pak choi stems and stir-fry until just starting to soften.
Add the noodles and pak choi leaves. Give the sauce a stir, pour it in and toss everything over the heat until the leaves have wilted and the sauce coats the noodles.
Divide between warm bowls and scatter with the spring onion greens.

tips: This quantity suits a standard wok. To serve four, cook it in two batches rather than doubling it in one pan, which would steam everything.

substitutions.use: shredded green cabbage or tenderstem broccoli

substitutions.note: soak or cook following the packet instructions

recipes.storage: Keeps for 2 days in the fridge. Reheat in a hot pan with a splash of water until piping hot.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Greek Salad
recipes.description: Chunky ripe tomatoes, cucumber, green pepper and Kalamata olives under a slab of feta, dressed with nothing more than good olive oil, a little vinegar and dried oregano.

items.prep: deseeded and sliced into thin rings

steps.text: Toss the sliced onion with the vinegar and a pinch of salt in a large serving bowl. Leave to soften and lose its raw bite while you prepare everything else.
Add the tomatoes to the bowl with another good pinch of salt and turn them over a couple of times so they start to give up their juice.
Add the cucumber, green pepper and olives. Pour over three-quarters of the oil and toss gently with your hands or a large spoon.
steps.tip: Go easy on the salt at this stage — the feta and olives bring plenty.

steps.text: Sit the feta on top in one piece, or broken into two or three large slabs. Rub the oregano between your fingers over the cheese and salad, then pour over the remaining oil.
Serve straight away with bread to mop up the juices at the bottom of the bowl.

tips: This salad is only as good as its tomatoes. Make it in summer and never chill them.
Buy feta in a block in brine; ready-crumbled feta is drier and blander.

substitutions.note: common on the islands

recipes.storage: Best eaten within an hour of making. Leftovers keep for a day in the fridge but the vegetables will soften.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Guacamole
recipes.description: Chunky, lime-bright guacamole built on a rough paste of onion, chilli, coriander and salt, so every spoonful of avocado is seasoned through. Ten minutes and no cooking.

items.prep: leaves and tender stalks, finely chopped

steps.text: Put the onion, chilli, half the coriander and the salt on a board or in a mortar. Crush with the flat of a knife or the pestle until you have a coarse, wet paste.
steps.tip: Crushing the aromatics with the salt releases their juices, which then season the avocado evenly instead of sitting in raw chunks.

steps.text: Halve and stone the avocados and scoop the flesh into a bowl. Add the paste and mash roughly with a fork, leaving plenty of texture; some lumps the size of a hazelnut are what you want.
Stir in the lime juice and the rest of the coriander. Taste with whatever you are serving it with and adjust the salt and lime — it usually needs more of both than you expect.
steps.tip: Tortilla chips are salty, so taste on a chip rather than off a spoon before adding more salt.

tips: A ripe avocado gives slightly when pressed gently near the stalk end. Rock-hard ones will not mash, and very soft ones are often brown inside.
If you like tomato in it, add one ripe tomato, deseeded and finely diced, at the very end so it does not make the guacamole watery.

substitutions.note: if you have no fresh chilli

recipes.storage: Best within an hour of making. To hold it for up to a day, press cling film directly onto the surface so no air reaches it and keep in the fridge; scrape off any browned top layer before serving.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Hummus
recipes.description: Silky, pale hummus with plenty of tahini and a clean lemon edge. Simmering tinned chickpeas until they collapse is what gets it properly smooth without peeling a single one.

steps.text: Put the drained chickpeas in a saucepan with the bicarbonate of soda and cover with water by about 3 cm. Bring to the boil, then simmer until the chickpeas are very soft and squash to a paste between your fingers. Skim off any foam and loose skins that float up.
steps.tip: This step is worth the time. The bicarbonate breaks down the skins, which is what makes the difference between grainy and smooth.

steps.text: Drain well and rinse briefly under hot water to wash off the bicarbonate. Set aside a spoonful of whole chickpeas for the top if you like.
Tip the warm chickpeas into a food processor and blend for a full minute, scraping down the sides, until you have a thick, stiff paste.

Add the tahini, lemon juice, garlic, salt and cumin and blend again. With the motor running, trickle in the ice-cold water a tablespoon at a time until the hummus turns pale, light and smooth, then keep blending for another 2–3 minutes.
steps.tip: Stop adding water when it is slightly looser than you want. It firms up as it cools.

steps.text: Taste and adjust with more salt or lemon. Spread into a shallow bowl, make a swirl with the back of a spoon, pour over the olive oil and dust with paprika.

tips: Tahini quality decides the flavour. Choose a pale, pourable one and stir the jar well before measuring; a dark, stiff tahini makes bitter hummus.
Serve at room temperature, not fridge-cold, when the flavour is fuller and the texture softer.

substitutions.note: soak overnight, then simmer with the bicarbonate for 40–60 minutes until collapsing

recipes.storage: Keeps in a sealed container in the fridge for up to 4 days. Stir in a splash of water to loosen and bring to room temperature before serving.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Kimchi Fried Rice
recipes.description: Yesterday's rice fried hard with ripe, sour kimchi and a spoonful of gochujang until sticky and crisp at the edges, then topped with a lacy fried egg.

items.prep: thinly sliced, white and green parts kept separate

items.note: plus 2 tbsp juice from the jar

steps.text: Break up the cold rice with damp fingers so there are no large clumps. Have everything else chopped and measured before you start, as this cooks quickly.
Heat 1 tbsp of the oil in a large frying pan or wok over a medium-high heat. Add the spring onion whites and garlic and stir-fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the kimchi and fry, stirring now and then, until it has darkened a shade and is starting to caramelise at the edges.
steps.tip: Do not cut this short. Cooking the kimchi down is what gives the rice its deep, rounded flavour rather than just sourness.

steps.text: Stir in the gochujang and kimchi juice, then add the rice. Turn the heat to high and stir-fry, pressing the rice into the pan and turning it over, until every grain is stained red and piping hot.
Add the soy sauce and sesame oil and toss well. Press the rice into an even layer and leave it untouched for a minute so the base crisps, then take off the heat.
Heat the remaining oil in a small frying pan over a medium-high heat and fry the eggs until the whites are set with frilly brown edges and the yolks are still runny, 2–3 minutes.
Divide the rice between two bowls, top each with an egg and scatter over the spring onion greens, sesame seeds and nori. Break the yolk into the rice as you eat.

tips: Use the oldest, sourest kimchi you have. Fresh kimchi is too mild and crunchy to stand up to frying.
Cool freshly cooked rice quickly, chill it within an hour and use it within a day. Warm, just-cooked rice turns to mush in the pan.
Most kimchi is made with fish sauce or salted shrimp. Look for a vegan one if you are cooking for vegetarians.

substitutions.use: 1 tsp chilli flakes and 1 tsp miso

substitutions.note: the result is a little less sticky

recipes.storage: Eat straight away. Do not keep or reheat leftovers, as the rice has already been cooled and reheated once.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Lamb Kofta with Yoghurt
recipes.description: Juicy spiced lamb kofta flecked with mint and parsley, charred on a hot griddle and served in warm pitta with garlicky lemon yoghurt, tomato and sumac onions.

items.note: half juiced, half cut into wedges

steps.text: Put all the kofta ingredients except the oil in a large bowl. Knead firmly with one hand for a couple of minutes until the mixture turns sticky and holds together as a paste.
steps.tip: Squeezing the grated onion dry and kneading properly are what stop kofta falling apart in the pan. Do not skip either.

steps.text: With damp hands, divide the mixture into 12 and shape each piece into a stubby sausage about 8 cm long. Lay on a plate, cover and chill to firm up.
While they chill, stir the yoghurt with the garlic, lemon juice, olive oil and salt. Toss the sliced red onion with the sumac and a small pinch of salt and set aside to soften.

Heat a griddle pan or heavy frying pan over a high heat until very hot. Brush the kofta with oil and cook, turning every couple of minutes, until well browned all over and cooked through with no pink in the centre.
steps.tip: Leave them alone for the first 2 minutes. They release from the pan by themselves once a crust has formed.

steps.text: Rest the kofta on a warm plate for 3 minutes. Meanwhile, warm the pittas in the hot pan or a toaster.
Split the pittas and fill with kofta, tomato, sumac onions, mint leaves and a generous spoonful of yoghurt. Serve with the lemon wedges.

equipment: griddle pan or heavy frying pan
tips: To barbecue, thread the mixture onto flat metal skewers and cook over hot coals for 8–10 minutes, turning often.
To oven-grill instead, cook on a rack under a hot grill for 10–12 minutes, turning once.

substitutions.use: beef mince or a half-and-half mix
substitutions.note: avoid extra-lean mince, which cooks up dry

recipes.storage: Cooked kofta keep for 3 days in the fridge; reheat in a hot oven until piping hot. Shaped raw kofta freeze well for up to 3 months — defrost fully before cooking.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Lemon and Garlic Chicken Traybake
recipes.description: Crisp-skinned chicken thighs roasted over potatoes that soak up the lemony, garlicky juices. One tin, very little washing up.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 220°C (200°C fan). Tip the potatoes, onions and garlic cloves into your largest roasting tin, add 2 tbsp of the oil and half the salt, and toss. Spread out in one layer and roast to give them a head start.
steps.tip: The tin needs to be big enough that nothing is piled up, or the potatoes will steam and stay pale.

steps.text: Meanwhile, zest one lemon into a bowl. Add the remaining oil, the oregano, the rest of the salt and plenty of pepper, then add the chicken and rub the mixture all over, including under the skin where you can. Juice the zested lemon into the stock. Cut the second lemon into 6 wedges.

Take the tin out of the oven and turn the potatoes. Tuck in the lemon wedges and thyme, then sit the chicken on top, skin-side up. Pour the lemony stock around the chicken rather than over it, so the skin stays dry.
Roast until the skin is deep golden and crisp and the juices run clear when you pierce the thickest thigh next to the bone. A probe thermometer should read at least 75°C.
steps.tip: If the skin is browning too quickly, move the tin down a shelf rather than covering it, which would soften the skin.

steps.text: Leave to rest in the tin. Squeeze the soft garlic out of its skins and stir it through the potatoes and pan juices along with the juice from a couple of the roasted lemon wedges.
Scatter with the parsley and serve straight from the tin, spooning the juices over everything.

tips: Take the chicken out of the fridge 20 minutes before cooking so it roasts evenly.
A green salad or some steamed greens is all this needs alongside.

substitutions.note: same timing

recipes.storage: Keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Reheat in a 200°C (180°C fan) oven for about 15 minutes, until the chicken is piping hot throughout.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Lemon Drizzle Cake
recipes.description: A buttery loaf scented with lemon zest, soaked while still warm with sharp lemon juice and sugar that sets into a crunchy, frosted crust.

items.note: unwaxed; keep the juice for the drizzle

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C (160°C fan). Butter a 900g (2lb) loaf tin and line it with a strip of baking paper that overhangs the two long sides.
Put the butter, caster sugar and lemon zest in a large bowl and beat with an electric whisk for 3–4 minutes, until very pale and fluffy. Scrape down the sides of the bowl once or twice as you go.
steps.tip: Rubbing the zest into the sugar with your fingertips first releases the oils and gives a stronger lemon flavour.

steps.text: Beat in the eggs one at a time, adding a spoonful of the flour with each to stop the mixture curdling. Sift in the remaining flour and the salt, then fold together gently with the milk until you have a smooth batter that drops easily off the spoon.
Spoon the batter into the tin and level the top. Bake on the middle shelf for 45–50 minutes, until golden, springy to the touch and a skewer pushed into the centre comes out clean.
steps.tip: Do not open the oven for the first 30 minutes or the cake may sink in the middle.

steps.text: While the cake bakes, squeeze the two zested lemons; you want about 5 tablespoons of juice. Just before the cake comes out, stir the juice into the granulated sugar. Do not let it dissolve, as the undissolved sugar is what gives the crunchy top.
As soon as the cake is out of the oven, prick it all over with a skewer, going right to the bottom. Spoon the drizzle slowly over the hot cake, letting each spoonful soak in before adding the next.
Leave the cake in its tin until completely cool and the top has set into a crisp sugar crust, about 1 hour. Lift out by the paper and slice.

tips: The butter must be properly soft, almost the texture of mayonnaise, or it will not cream to the pale, airy stage the cake depends on.
Pour the drizzle while the cake is hot. A cold cake will not absorb the juice and the syrup will run off.

substitutions.use: plain flour plus 2 tsp baking powder

substitutions.note: an orange drizzle will be sweeter and less sharp

recipes.storage: Keeps in an airtight tin for 4 days. Freeze, well wrapped, for up to 3 months.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Maple Pecan Granola
recipes.description: Crisp, clumpy granola baked low and slow with maple syrup, toasted pecans and a warm note of cinnamon. Left to cool untouched on the tray, it breaks into proper clusters.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C (140°C fan). Line a large, rimmed baking tray with baking paper.

Mix the oats, pecans, pumpkin seeds, cinnamon and salt in a large bowl. Whisk the maple syrup, oil and vanilla together in a jug, pour over the dry ingredients and stir thoroughly until every oat looks damp and glossy.
Tip onto the tray and spread into an even layer about 1 cm deep, then press it down firmly with the back of a spoon so it is compacted.
steps.tip: Pressing the mixture down is what makes clusters. Loose granola bakes into separate flakes.

steps.text: Bake for 20 minutes, then turn the tray around. Gently turn the granola over in large sections with a fish slice, bringing the darker edges into the middle, and press it flat again.
Bake for a further 12–15 minutes until evenly golden brown and smelling toasty. It will still feel soft when hot; it crisps as it cools.
steps.tip: Go by colour, not texture. Pull it out when it is the shade of a digestive biscuit; maple syrup turns bitter quickly once it goes past that.

steps.text: Leave to cool completely on the tray without stirring. Once cold and hard, break into clusters with your hands and mix in the raisins, if using.

tips: Never bake the dried fruit. It scorches and turns hard, so always add it once the granola is cold.
If your tray is small, use two. A layer much deeper than 1 cm steams and stays chewy in the middle.

substitutions.note: roughly chopped

substitutions.use: melted coconut oil or sunflower oil

recipes.storage: Keep in an airtight jar at room temperature for up to 3 weeks. If it softens, re-crisp on a tray at 150°C (130°C fan) for 5 minutes and cool again.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Masala Chai
recipes.description: Strong black tea simmered with fresh ginger, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and peppercorns, then boiled up with milk until creamy and fragrant. Warming, spicy and as sweet as you like it.

items.note: loose-leaf Assam, or 3 strong tea bags

steps.text: Lightly crush the cardamom pods, cloves and peppercorns with a pestle and mortar or the base of a heavy pan, just enough to split the pods open. Snap the cinnamon stick in half.
Put the crushed spices, cinnamon, ginger and water in a small saucepan. Bring to the boil, then turn the heat down and simmer gently for 5 minutes so the spices infuse the water.
Add the tea and simmer for 2 minutes, until the liquid is a deep reddish brown.
steps.tip: Do not leave the tea much longer at this stage or the chai will turn bitter and tannic.

steps.text: Pour in the milk and bring back up to the boil, watching closely as it will rise up the pan quickly. Lower the heat and simmer for 3 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chai is the colour of caramel.
steps.tip: Letting it rise and then lifting the pan off the heat two or three times gives a richer, creamier cup.

steps.text: Stir in sugar to taste, then strain through a fine sieve or tea strainer into two mugs. Serve straight away.

tips: A little sugar is traditional and rounds out the spices; even if you normally take tea unsweetened, try a teaspoon.
Use a strong, malty tea such as Assam. Delicate teas like Darjeeling or Earl Grey are lost against the milk and spice.

substitutions.note: heat gently and do not boil hard, as it can split
stir honey in off the heat

recipes.storage: Best drunk fresh. The strained chai keeps in the fridge for 2 days; reheat gently or pour it over ice.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Mint Lemonade
recipes.description: Freshly squeezed lemons sweetened with a mint-steeped syrup and topped up with cold water over plenty of ice. Sharp, green and properly thirst-quenching.

items.note: a large handful, stalks and all

steps.text: Set aside a few of the best mint sprigs for serving. Put the sugar and 100ml water in a small saucepan over a medium heat and stir until the sugar has completely dissolved and the syrup is just starting to simmer, 2–3 minutes. Take it off the heat.
Bruise the rest of the mint by scrunching it in your hands, then push it under the surface of the hot syrup. Leave to steep for 15 minutes.
steps.tip: Add the mint off the heat. Boiling it gives a dull, stewed flavour instead of a fresh one.

steps.text: Meanwhile, juice 4 of the lemons; you want about 180ml. Rolling them firmly on the worktop first helps them give up more juice. Thinly slice the remaining lemon.
Strain the syrup through a sieve into a large jug, pressing on the mint to extract all the liquid. Stir in the lemon juice and the cold water.
Taste and adjust. Add a splash more water if it is too sharp or strong, or a squeeze more lemon if too sweet. Chill for 30 minutes if you have time.
steps.tip: Make it a touch stronger than you think it should be, as the ice will dilute it.

steps.text: Fill four tall glasses with ice, add the lemon slices and reserved mint sprigs, and pour over the lemonade. If you are using sparkling water, add it at the last moment so it keeps its fizz.

tips: For a slushy, vivid green version, blend the finished lemonade with two large handfuls of ice and a few extra mint leaves, then serve at once.
Lemons vary a great deal in size and sharpness, so trust your taste over the measurements.

substitutions.note: use 80g; the lemonade will no longer be vegan
you will need about 8 for the same amount of juice

recipes.storage: The undiluted base of syrup and lemon juice keeps in the fridge for 5 days. Once diluted, drink within 2 days.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Miso Soup with Tofu
recipes.description: A proper dashi made from kombu and bonito, with soft cubes of silken tofu, wakame and white miso whisked in off the heat. Quiet, savoury and far better than anything from a sachet.

steps.text: Put the kombu and cold water in a saucepan and leave to soak. This is where most of the flavour is drawn out, and it needs no attention.
steps.tip: Do not wash off the white bloom on the kombu — it is full of savoury flavour. A wipe with a damp cloth is enough.

steps.text: Set the pan over a low heat and bring it slowly up to the point where small bubbles gather at the edge, taking about 10 minutes. Lift out the kombu just before it boils.
Bring the liquid to a simmer, scatter in the bonito flakes and turn off the heat. Leave them to steep and sink.

Meanwhile, cover the wakame with cold water in a small bowl and leave to swell for 5 minutes, then drain. Strain the dashi through a fine sieve into a jug, pressing lightly on the flakes, and return it to the rinsed pan.
Warm the dashi over a low heat until steaming. Add the tofu and wakame and heat gently for 2 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat. Put the miso in a ladle or small bowl, whisk in a little of the hot dashi until smooth, then stir it into the soup. Taste and add a touch more miso if you like.
steps.tip: Never boil the soup once the miso is in. It dulls the aroma and makes the texture grainy.

steps.text: Ladle into small bowls, dividing the tofu evenly, and scatter with the spring onions. Serve straight away.

tips: Stir the soup just before each sip. Miso settles naturally.
Miso varies a great deal in saltiness, so start with 3 tbsp if yours is a darker type.

substitutions.use: 3 dried shiitake mushrooms soaked with the kombu
substitutions.note: makes the soup vegan

substitutions.use: 1 litre water with 2 tsp instant dashi powder

recipes.storage: Best eaten as soon as it is made. The dashi alone keeps for 3 days in the fridge; add miso and tofu when you reheat it.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Mushroom Risotto
recipes.description: Creamy, loose risotto with mushrooms fried separately until properly golden, so they stay meaty instead of going soft and grey. Finished with butter, parmesan and thyme.

steps.text: Bring the stock to a simmer in a saucepan, then keep it on the lowest heat so it stays hot.
steps.tip: Cold stock stalls the cooking every time you add it, so keeping it hot matters.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp of the oil and about a third of the butter in a wide, heavy pan over a high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer, in two batches if needed, and leave them alone for a couple of minutes before stirring. Cook until golden and any liquid has evaporated, then add the garlic and thyme for the final minute. Season and tip onto a plate.
Turn the heat down to medium-low and add the remaining oil and the onion to the same pan with a pinch of salt. Cook until soft and translucent but not coloured.
Add the rice and stir for a couple of minutes until the grains are hot and look glassy at the edges. Pour in the wine and stir until it has almost all been absorbed.

Add the hot stock a ladleful at a time, stirring often and waiting until each addition is nearly absorbed before adding the next. Keep it at a steady, gentle bubble. Start tasting after 16 minutes. The rice is ready when it is tender with a slight bite in the centre, and you may not need all the stock.
Stir in most of the mushrooms. The risotto should be loose enough to flow slowly when you tilt the pan, so add a last splash of stock if it is stiff.
Take the pan off the heat. Beat in the remaining butter and the parmesan, cover and leave to rest.
steps.tip: Beating the butter and cheese in off the heat is what makes the risotto creamy rather than greasy.

steps.text: Taste and season with salt and pepper. Spoon into warm bowls and top with the reserved mushrooms, the parsley and more parmesan.

tips: Risotto carries on thickening on the plate, so serve it a little looser than you think it should be.
Check the label of your stock if you are cooking gluten-free, as some cubes contain wheat.

substitutions.use: a mix of wild or portobello mushrooms

substitutions.note: finish with a squeeze of lemon juice
traditional parmesan is made with animal rennet

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away. Leftovers keep for 1 day in the fridge if cooled quickly, and must be reheated until piping hot with a splash of stock or water.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: No-Knead Bread
recipes.description: Four ingredients, two minutes of stirring and a long overnight rest give a crackling, blistered crust and an open, chewy crumb. Time does all the work that kneading normally would.

steps.text: Put the flour, salt and yeast in a large bowl and stir them together. Pour in the water and mix with a wooden spoon or your hand until there are no dry patches left. The dough will be rough, wet and sticky; that is how it should look.

Cover the bowl with a plate or a damp tea towel and leave at room temperature for 12–18 hours. It is ready when it has more than doubled, the surface is covered in bubbles and it wobbles when you shake the bowl.
steps.tip: In a warm kitchen (above about 24°C) start checking after 8–10 hours, as the dough will move much faster.

steps.text: Flour the worktop generously and scrape the dough out onto it. With floured hands, fold the edges into the middle four or five times to make a rough ball, then turn it seam-side down onto a large square of baking paper. Dust the top with flour, cover loosely with a tea towel and leave to rise for 1 hour.
steps.tip: Handle the dough gently and quickly. You are shaping it, not knocking the air out.

steps.text: When the second rise has 30 minutes left, put a lidded cast-iron casserole (about 24cm, 4–5 litres) into the oven and heat it to 230°C (210°C fan). The pot must be thoroughly hot before the dough goes in.

Carefully lift the pot out of the oven and take off the lid. Slash the top of the loaf once with a sharp knife, then lower the dough in on its baking paper. Put the lid back on and bake for 30 minutes.
steps.tip: The pot and its lid are dangerously hot. Leave an oven glove resting on the lid so nobody grabs it bare-handed.

steps.text: Remove the lid and bake for a further 12–15 minutes, until the crust is a deep chestnut brown and the loaf sounds hollow when tapped underneath.
Lift the loaf onto a wire rack and leave it to cool for at least 1 hour before cutting. The crumb is still setting while it cools, and slicing early leaves it gummy.

tips: Mix the dough in the evening and you can bake it for lunch the next day.
For more flavour, leave the mixed dough in the fridge for up to 3 days instead, then let it come to room temperature for 2 hours before shaping.

substitutions.use: half strong white and half wholemeal flour
substitutions.note: add 25ml more water
check the lid handle is safe at 230°C

recipes.storage: Keep cut-side down on a board or in a paper bag for up to 3 days. Freeze sliced for up to 3 months and toast from frozen.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Overnight Oats
recipes.description: Oats soaked overnight in milk and yoghurt until soft and creamy, with chia seeds for body and a little maple syrup. Five minutes in the evening, breakfast ready when you wake.

steps.text: Put the oats, chia seeds and salt in a bowl or divide them between two jars. Add the milk, yoghurt, maple syrup and vanilla and stir well, scraping the bottom so no dry pockets of oats or clumps of chia are left.
steps.tip: Stir again after 5 minutes if you can. Chia seeds clump as they start to swell and a second stir keeps the texture even.

steps.text: Cover and chill overnight. The oats will absorb most of the liquid and the mixture will set to a thick, spoonable consistency.
In the morning, stir and loosen with a splash of milk if it is thicker than you like. Top with the blueberries and a little more maple syrup.

tips: Use rolled (porridge) oats, not jumbo or instant. Jumbo oats stay chewy and instant oats turn to paste.
In a hurry, 2 hours in the fridge is enough for the oats to soften, though the texture is better after a full night.

substitutions.note: makes it dairy-free and vegan; the result is slightly looser
add banana in the morning so it does not brown

recipes.storage: Keeps covered in the fridge for up to 3 days. Add fresh fruit just before eating.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Roast Aubergine with Tahini and Pomegranate
recipes.description: Wedges of aubergine roasted until soft and caramelised, piled onto a platter with spiced crisp chickpeas, a lemony tahini sauce and bright pomegranate seeds.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 220°C (200°C fan). Toss the aubergine wedges with 4 tbsp of the oil and the flaky salt on a large baking tray, then arrange them cut-side down in a single layer. Roast on the top shelf.
steps.tip: Use two trays if the wedges are touching. Crowded aubergine goes soft and pale instead of browning.

steps.text: Meanwhile, toss the dried chickpeas with the remaining oil, the cumin, smoked paprika and a pinch of salt on a second, smaller tray.

Turn the aubergine wedges over and return them to the oven with the tray of chickpeas on the shelf below. Roast until the aubergine is deep golden and completely soft when pierced with a knife, and the chickpeas are crisp.

While everything roasts, whisk the tahini, lemon juice, garlic and salt together in a bowl. It will seize and thicken at first. Whisk in the cold water a tablespoon at a time until the sauce is smooth, pale and the consistency of pouring cream.
steps.tip: Tahini brands differ in thickness, so judge the water by eye rather than by the measurement.

steps.text: Spread half the tahini sauce over a large platter. Arrange the aubergine on top, scatter over the chickpeas and drizzle with the remaining sauce.
Finish with the pomegranate seeds, parsley, mint and sumac. Serve warm or at room temperature.

tips: To get the seeds out of a pomegranate without mess, halve it, hold a half cut-side down over a bowl and hit the back firmly with a wooden spoon.
Warm flatbreads or steamed rice make this a more filling meal, though flatbreads mean it is no longer gluten-free.

substitutions.note: do not roast them, just warm through and scatter over

recipes.storage: Keeps for 3 days in the fridge, with the sauce and herbs stored separately. Bring back to room temperature before serving; the chickpeas will lose their crispness.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Roasted Tomato Soup
recipes.description: Tomatoes, red onion and whole garlic cloves roasted until soft and charred at the edges, then blended into a soup that tastes far richer than its short ingredient list suggests.

items.note: plus a few small leaves to serve
only if the tomatoes are sharp

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200°C (180°C fan). Spread the tomatoes cut-side up in a large roasting tin with the onion wedges, garlic cloves and thyme. Drizzle with the oil, season generously with salt and pepper and toss the onions to coat.
steps.tip: Use a tin big enough for a single layer. Crowded tomatoes steam instead of roasting.

steps.text: Roast until the tomatoes have slumped and the onions are soft and catching at the edges.
Squeeze the soft garlic out of its skins into a large saucepan and discard the skins and thyme stalks. Scrape in the tomatoes, onions and every bit of juice from the tin.
Stir in the tomato purée and hot stock, bring to a simmer and cook gently to bring everything together.
Take off the heat, add the basil and blend until completely smooth. Stir in the balsamic vinegar, taste, and adjust with salt, pepper and the sugar if it needs it.
steps.tip: For a silky finish, push the soup through a sieve to catch the skins and seeds.

steps.text: Ladle into warm bowls and finish with a thread of olive oil, a few basil leaves and black pepper.

tips: This is forgiving of mediocre tomatoes — roasting concentrates what flavour they have — but in winter swap a third of them for a tin of good plum tomatoes added with the stock.
Stock cubes vary, so check the label if you are cooking gluten-free.

substitutions.use: a spoonful of pesto stirred in at the end
substitutions.note: no longer vegan or nut-free

recipes.storage: Keeps for 4 days in the fridge and freezes well for up to 3 months. Thin with a splash of water when reheating.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Rosemary Focaccia
recipes.description: A wet, olive-oil-rich dough that bakes into a bubbly, open crumb with a crisp golden base, dimpled with rosemary and flaky salt. No kneading, just a few folds.

items.note: for the tin and the top

steps.text: Mix the flour, yeast and fine salt in a large bowl. Pour in the water and 2 tablespoons of oil and stir with a wooden spoon until there is no dry flour left. The dough will be very wet and sticky, closer to a thick batter than a bread dough. Cover and leave for 15 minutes.

With a wet hand, reach under one side of the dough, stretch it upwards and fold it over the top. Give the bowl a quarter turn and repeat, working round until you have made 8 folds and the dough feels tighter and smoother.
steps.tip: Wet hands stop the dough sticking far better than flour, and adding flour would make the bread heavier.

steps.text: Cover the bowl and leave somewhere warm for 1–1½ hours, until the dough has doubled in size and is full of bubbles.

Pour 2 tablespoons of the topping oil into a 20 x 30cm baking tin with sides at least 4cm deep, and rub it over the base and sides. Scrape the dough into the tin, turn it over once to coat it in oil, then gently stretch it towards the corners. If it springs back, leave it for 10 minutes and try again.
Cover the tin and leave for 45 minutes, until the dough is puffy, fills the tin and wobbles when shaken. Meanwhile, heat the oven to 220°C (200°C fan).

Drizzle the remaining 2 tablespoons of oil over the dough. Oil your fingers and press them straight down to the bottom of the tin all over, making deep dimples. Scatter over the rosemary leaves and the flaky salt.
steps.tip: Toss the rosemary in a little oil first so it crisps in the oven instead of scorching.

steps.text: Bake for 22–25 minutes, until deep golden on top and crisp underneath. Lift a corner with a palette knife to check the base is browned.
Lift the focaccia out of the tin onto a wire rack straight away so the base stays crisp. Leave for 15 minutes before cutting into squares.

tips: For better flavour, do the first rise overnight in the fridge (8–18 hours), then let the dough sit in the oiled tin for about 2 hours until puffy before dimpling.
A metal tin gives a crisper base than ceramic or glass.

substitutions.use: halved cherry tomatoes and olives pressed into the dimples
substitutions.note: keep a little salt on top as well

recipes.storage: Best on the day it is baked. Wrap leftovers and keep for 2 days, reviving in a hot oven for 5 minutes. Freezes well for up to 2 months.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Shakshuka
