recipes.description: Eggs poached in a thick, smoky tomato and pepper sauce until the whites are set and the yolks still run. Bring the pan to the table and mop it up with bread.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a frying pan about 24cm wide over a medium heat. Add the onion and pepper with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring now and then, until very soft and starting to colour.
Add the garlic, cumin, both paprikas and the chilli flakes and stir for a minute until fragrant. Stir in the tomato puree.

Pour in the chopped tomatoes and water, then add the sugar and salt. Simmer, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is thick enough that a spoon dragged through it leaves a clear trail. Taste and adjust the seasoning now, before the eggs go in.
steps.tip: A thin sauce will not hold the eggs in place, so keep going until it is properly thick.

steps.text: Turn the heat down to low. Make four wells in the sauce with the back of a spoon and crack an egg into each. Season the eggs with a little salt.
steps.tip: Crack each egg into a cup first if you are worried about shell or a broken yolk.

steps.text: Cover the pan and cook gently until the whites are just set and the yolks still wobble. Start checking after 5 minutes, as the eggs carry on cooking once off the heat.
Scatter with the feta and coriander and serve straight from the pan with the toasted bread.

tips: No lid for your pan? A baking tray or a large plate laid over the top does the job.
To serve four, double everything and use a 30cm pan so the eggs have room.

substitutions.note: add a spoonful on top at the end
stir 1 to 2 tsp in with the tomato puree

recipes.storage: The sauce keeps for 4 days in the fridge without the eggs. Reheat it until bubbling, then add fresh eggs.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Slow-Cooked Tomato Sauce
recipes.description: Tinned plum tomatoes simmered gently for over an hour with soft onion, garlic and olive oil until thick, sweet and deep red. A patient, all-purpose sauce for pasta, pizza or the freezer.

items.note: use it to rinse out the tins
only if the sauce tastes sharp

steps.text: Warm the olive oil in a wide, heavy-based saucepan over a medium-low heat. Add the onion and half the salt and cook gently, stirring now and then, until completely soft, translucent and sweet but not browned.
steps.tip: Do not rush this. Onion that is still firm when the tomatoes go in stays firm, because the acid stops it softening.

steps.text: Add the garlic and cook for a minute until fragrant. Stir in the tomato purée and cook for 2 minutes more, stirring, until it darkens a shade and starts to catch on the base of the pan.
Add the tomatoes and crush them against the side of the pan with a wooden spoon. Swill out the tins with the water and add that too, along with the bay leaf and the remaining salt. Bring to a simmer.

Turn the heat down as low as it will go, so the surface only blips occasionally, and set a lid on the pan slightly ajar. Cook, stirring every 15 minutes or so and scraping the base, until the sauce is thick and glossy and the oil has started to separate around the edges.
steps.tip: If it thickens too much or begins to stick before the time is up, add a splash of water and lower the heat further.

steps.text: Fish out the bay leaf. Taste and adjust with more salt, and a pinch of sugar only if it is still sharp. Tear in the basil. Leave the sauce chunky, or blend it with a stick blender if you want it smooth.

tips: Whole tinned plum tomatoes generally taste better and break down more readily than ready-chopped ones, which are often firmer and more watery.
The sauce doubles well in a larger pan and is worth making in bulk; allow an extra 15–20 minutes of simmering.

substitutions.note: reduce the water to 100 ml and the simmering time to about 45 minutes
add it with the tomatoes rather than at the end

recipes.storage: Cool, then keep in the fridge for up to 5 days or freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat gently with a splash of water.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Smash Burgers
recipes.description: Thin patties pressed hard onto a ferociously hot pan so the edges turn lacy and deeply browned, stacked two to a bun with melted cheese and a sharp burger sauce.

steps.text: Stir the burger sauce ingredients together in a small bowl. Prepare the onion, gherkins and lettuce so the toppings are ready before you start cooking.
Divide the mince into 8 equal portions of about 75g and roll each very loosely into a ball. Do not season or compact them. Keep them in the fridge until the pan is hot.
steps.tip: Cold, loosely packed mince smashes into a ragged-edged patty. Overworked mince turns dense and bouncy.

steps.text: Set a cast-iron or heavy-based frying pan over a medium heat and toast the buns cut-side down until golden. Set them aside.
Turn the heat up to high and let the dry pan heat until it is just starting to smoke. Open a window or switch on the extractor fan.

Put 2 or 3 balls of mince in the pan, well spaced. Lay a square of baking paper over each one and press down hard with a sturdy spatula until the patty is about 5mm thick, then peel off the paper. Season generously with salt and pepper and cook without moving until the edges are dark brown and crisp.
steps.tip: Smash within the first 30 seconds only. Pressing later squeezes out the juices.

steps.text: Scrape firmly under each patty to keep the crust attached and flip. Lay a slice of cheddar on each straight away and cook until the cheese has melted.
Stack the patties in pairs and keep them warm on a plate while you cook the rest, scraping the pan clean of any burnt bits between batches.
Spread sauce on both halves of each bun. Add lettuce and a double patty to each base, top with the chopped onion and gherkin slices, then close and serve immediately.

tips: Do not use lean mince. The fat is what fries the patty from underneath and makes the crust.
No oil is needed in a seasoned cast-iron pan. In a stainless steel pan, wipe on the thinnest film of vegetable oil first.

substitutions.note: they melt more smoothly

recipes.storage: Best eaten the moment they are assembled. The sauce keeps for 5 days in the fridge.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Smoky Beef Chilli
recipes.description: A dark, thick chilli with properly browned mince, smoked paprika and a spoonful of cocoa for depth. It needs time rather than effort, and tastes even better reheated.

steps.text: Heat half the oil in a large casserole over a high heat. Add half the mince, press it into a flat layer and leave it without stirring until the underside is dark brown. Break it up, cook for a couple of minutes more, then tip into a bowl. Repeat with the remaining mince, without adding more oil.
steps.tip: Grey, steamed mince makes a flat-tasting chilli. Let it get genuinely brown and a bit crusty.

steps.text: Turn the heat down to medium and add the remaining oil, the onions and the peppers with a pinch of salt. Cook, scraping up the browned bits, until soft.
Add the garlic, smoked paprika, cumin, chilli powder, oregano and cinnamon and stir for a minute. Add the tomato puree and cook, stirring, for a minute more.
Return the mince to the pan. Add the chopped tomatoes, stock, cocoa and salt and stir well. Bring to the boil, then turn the heat down low, part-cover with the lid and simmer, stirring occasionally.

Stir in the kidney beans and simmer with the lid off until the chilli is thick and glossy and a spoon dragged across the base leaves a trail. Meanwhile, cook the rice following the packet instructions.
Take the chilli off the heat, stir in the lime juice and leave it to stand. Taste and adjust the salt and heat.
Serve over the rice with the coriander scattered on top.

tips: Start with 1 tsp of chilli powder if you are feeding children, and put hot sauce on the table for everyone else.
Make it a day ahead if you can. The flavours round out overnight in the fridge.

substitutions.note: use 20g, and check it is dairy-free if that matters

substitutions.use: pork mince or a half-and-half mix

recipes.storage: Keeps for 4 days in the fridge or 3 months in the freezer, without the rice. Defrost fully and reheat until piping hot.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Soy and Ginger Glazed Salmon
recipes.description: Crisp-skinned salmon lacquered in a sticky soy, honey and ginger glaze that reduces in the pan in a couple of minutes. Served with jasmine rice and pak choi cooked in what is left behind.

steps.text: Rinse the rice in a sieve until the water runs mostly clear. Put it in a small saucepan with the measured water, bring to the boil, then cover with a tight lid and cook on the lowest heat.
Take the rice off the heat and leave it to steam with the lid on until you are ready to serve.
While the rice cooks, stir all the glaze ingredients together in a small bowl. Pat the salmon very dry with kitchen paper, especially the skin.
steps.tip: Dry skin is the difference between crisp and flabby, and it also stops the fish sticking.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a non-stick frying pan over a medium-high heat. Lay the salmon in skin-side down, press each fillet flat with a spatula for the first 10 seconds, then leave it alone until the skin is crisp and the flesh has turned opaque about two-thirds of the way up the sides.

Turn the heat down to medium and flip the salmon. Pour the glaze around the fish and let it bubble, spooning it over the fillets, until it is syrupy and the salmon is just cooked through. Lift the salmon onto warm plates.
steps.tip: The honey catches quickly. If the glaze is thickening too fast, add a tablespoon of water and pull the pan off the heat.

steps.text: Put the pak choi cut-side down in the same pan, add 2 tbsp of water and cover with a lid or a plate. Steam until the stems are just tender, turning once to coat in the sticky pan juices.
Fluff the rice with a fork and serve with the salmon and pak choi. Spoon over any glaze left in the pan and scatter with the spring onions and sesame seeds.

equipment: non-stick frying pan with a lid
tips: Fillets of even thickness cook most evenly. For a very thick piece, give the skin side an extra minute.

substitutions.note: steam for 4 to 5 minutes
makes the dish gluten-free if the tamari is labelled so

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Leftover salmon keeps for 1 day in the fridge and is good cold, flaked over rice or salad.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Tabbouleh
recipes.description: A herb salad, not a grain one — heaps of finely cut parsley and mint with tomato, spring onion and just enough bulgur to soak up the lemon and olive oil.

steps.text: Put the bulgur in a large bowl with the diced tomatoes, all their juices and the lemon juice. Stir and leave so the grains swell and soften in the liquid.
steps.tip: This only works with fine bulgur. If yours is coarse, cover it with boiling water for 15 minutes, drain well and squeeze dry before mixing with the tomatoes.

steps.text: Meanwhile, wash the parsley and mint and dry them completely in a salad spinner or between clean tea towels. Trim off the thick lower parsley stalks, keeping the tender upper ones.
steps.tip: Wet herbs turn to mush under the knife and make a watery salad, so take your time here.

steps.text: Gather the parsley into a tight bundle and slice it as finely as you can with a sharp knife, working through it once rather than chopping back and forth. Stack and shred the mint leaves in the same way.
Add the herbs and spring onions to the bulgur and tomatoes. Pour over the olive oil, add the allspice if using, the salt and a few grinds of pepper, and toss lightly with a fork.
Taste and adjust — it should be bright and sharp, so add more lemon or salt if it seems flat. Serve within the hour, with crisp lettuce leaves for scooping if you like.

tips: Resist the food processor. It bruises the herbs and turns them dark and wet; a sharp knife keeps them fluffy and green.

substitutions.note: makes it gluten-free; use about 100 g cooked
very finely chopped

recipes.storage: Best on the day it is made. Leftovers keep for a day in the fridge; refresh with a squeeze of lemon.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Tarka Dal
recipes.description: Red lentils simmered with turmeric until they fall apart, then woken up with a sizzling pan of cumin, mustard seeds, garlic and chilli poured over at the last moment.

items.prep: rinsed until the water runs clear

steps.text: Put the rinsed lentils in a large saucepan with the water and turmeric. Bring to the boil, skim off the foam that rises, then turn the heat down to a steady simmer.
Simmer with the lid ajar, stirring now and then, until the lentils have completely broken down. Add the tomatoes and salt for the final 10 minutes.
steps.tip: Give it a hard whisk at the end for a smooth, creamy dal. Loosen with a splash of boiling water if it is thicker than you like.

steps.text: While the lentils finish, heat the oil in a frying pan over a medium-high heat. Add the cumin and mustard seeds and let them sizzle until the mustard seeds start to pop, about 30 seconds.
Add the onion and fry, stirring often, until deep golden at the edges.
Add the garlic, ginger and green chillies and fry for 2 minutes until the garlic is pale gold. Take the pan off the heat and stir in the chilli powder and garam masala.
steps.tip: Ground spices scorch in seconds, which is why they go in off the heat.

steps.text: Tip most of the tarka, oil and all, into the lentils and stir it through. Squeeze in the lemon juice, taste and add more salt if needed.
Spoon into bowls and top with the remaining tarka and the coriander. Serve with rice or flatbreads.

tips: Dal thickens a lot as it sits. Always loosen leftovers with water when reheating.
Slitting the chillies rather than chopping them gives fragrance with gentle heat. Chop them if you want it fiery.

substitutions.note: traditional, but no longer vegan or dairy-free

recipes.storage: Keeps for 4 days in the fridge or 3 months in the freezer. Reheat gently with a splash of water until piping hot.
recipes.author: Simmer

recipes.title: Thai Green Chicken Curry
recipes.description: Fragrant, creamy and as fiery as your curry paste allows, with tender chicken thighs and vegetables that keep their bite. On the table in the time it takes to cook the rice.

items.note: Thai basil if you can find it

steps.text: Rinse the rice in a sieve until the water runs mostly clear. Put it in a saucepan with the measured water and a pinch of salt, bring to the boil, then cover with a tight lid and turn the heat to its lowest setting.
Take the rice off the heat and leave it to steam with the lid on while you finish the curry. Do not lift the lid.

While the rice cooks, heat the oil in a wok or deep frying pan over a medium heat. Spoon in the thick cream from the top of the coconut milk tin along with the curry paste. Fry, stirring, until it smells fragrant and the oil starts to separate at the edges.
steps.tip: Start with 3 tbsp of paste if you do not know the brand. You can stir in more later, but you cannot take it out.

steps.text: Add the chicken and stir to coat it in the paste. Pour in the rest of the coconut milk and the stock, then add the fish sauce and sugar. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook, uncovered.
Add the green beans and courgette and simmer until the vegetables are just tender and the chicken is cooked through with no pink in the middle.
Take the pan off the heat. Stir in the lime juice and most of the basil, then taste. It should be salty, sour, sweet and hot all at once, so add a little more fish sauce, lime or sugar until it is.
Fluff the rice with a fork and serve the curry alongside, topped with the remaining basil and the sliced chilli if using.

tips: Keep the curry at a gentle simmer. A hard boil toughens the chicken and can make the coconut milk split.
Shop-bought pastes vary a lot in salt and heat, which is why the final tasting matters more than the measurements.

substitutions.note: add them with the vegetables, they need only 3 to 4 minutes
cut into 2cm cubes and add with the chicken
the dish is then no longer gluten-free

recipes.storage: Keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Reheat gently until piping hot. Cool leftover rice quickly, refrigerate within an hour and eat within a day.

recipes.title: Tomato Bruschetta
recipes.description: Charred toast rubbed with raw garlic and piled with salted ripe tomatoes, basil and good olive oil. It is only as good as the tomatoes, so make it in summer.

steps.text: Cut the tomatoes into roughly 1 cm dice, discarding the hard cores. Toss with the salt in a sieve set over a bowl and leave to drain.
steps.tip: Salting draws out the watery juice so the flavour is concentrated and the toast stays crisp.

steps.text: Tip the drained tomatoes into a bowl and stir in the 2 tbsp of olive oil, the vinegar if your tomatoes need sharpening, and a grind of black pepper. Tear in the basil. Taste and add more salt if needed.
Heat a griddle pan over a high heat or turn the grill to its highest setting. Toast the bread until crisp and charred in places on the outside but still a little chewy within, 1–2 minutes each side.
While the toast is hot, rub one side of each slice with the cut face of the garlic — the rough surface acts as a grater — then drizzle with the remaining oil.
steps.tip: Two or three firm strokes per slice is plenty. Raw garlic is strong and it should sit in the background.

steps.text: Spoon the tomatoes onto the toasts and serve immediately, before the bread softens.

tips: Never use tomatoes straight from the fridge; cold mutes their flavour. Leave them out for at least an hour first.
The salty tomato juice left in the bowl is too good to waste. Whisk it into a salad dressing.

substitutions.note: quartered; usually the best choice outside high summer
sliced on the diagonal

recipes.storage: Assemble just before eating. The dressed tomatoes will keep, covered at room temperature, for up to 2 hours; add the basil at the last minute.

recipes.title: Vanilla Panna Cotta
recipes.description: Barely set cream flecked with vanilla, with just enough gelatine to hold a gentle wobble when turned out. Ten minutes of work, then the fridge does the rest.

items.note: standard supermarket leaves, about 5g in total
a few drops for the moulds

steps.text: Put the gelatine leaves in a bowl of cold water, making sure they are fully submerged, and leave to soften for 5 minutes. Very lightly oil four 150ml ramekins or dariole moulds with a piece of kitchen paper.

Put the cream, milk, sugar and vanilla in a saucepan over a medium-low heat. Warm, stirring, until the sugar has dissolved and the mixture is steaming with small bubbles at the edge. Take it off the heat before it boils.
steps.tip: Boiling is unnecessary and can weaken the set. Steaming hot is all you need to dissolve the gelatine.

steps.text: Lift the gelatine out of the water and squeeze it firmly to get rid of the excess. Drop it into the hot cream and stir for a minute until it has completely dissolved.
Strain the mixture through a fine sieve into a jug. Leave it to cool for 15 minutes, stirring once or twice, so the vanilla seeds stay suspended and do not all sink to the bottom.
Stir once more, pour into the moulds and cover. Chill for at least 4 hours, or overnight, until set with a gentle wobble.
To turn out, dip each mould into a bowl of hot water for 5–10 seconds, run the tip of a knife around the top edge, then invert onto a plate and give it a firm shake. Serve with the raspberries.
steps.tip: If one refuses to budge, dip it again for a few seconds. Too long in the water and the outside will melt.

tips: Gelatine leaves vary in size and strength between brands. If yours are noticeably larger than about 7 x 11cm, weigh out 5g.
Not confident about turning them out? Set the panna cotta in glasses and serve it as it is.

substitutions.note: infuse the pod in the warm cream and remove it when you strain

substitutions.use: poached rhubarb, roasted plums or a spoonful of berry compote

recipes.storage: Keep covered in the fridge for up to 3 days. Turn out just before serving. Not suitable for freezing.
